q-2621.name: Question 1
q-2621.worked_solution:
Let $u=4-x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
$x=4-u.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x+1)\sqrt{4-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2(4-u)+1)\sqrt{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int (9-2u)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int (9{u}^{1/2}-2{u}^{3/2})\text{d}u \\  & =-(6{u}^{3/2}-\frac{4}{5}{u}^{5/2})+C \\  & =-6\sqrt{(4-x)^{3}}+\frac{4}{5}\sqrt{(4-x)^{5}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-49389.problem: Given that $u=1+{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to $\int {x}^{5}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x?$
q-49389.worked_solution:
Since $u=1+{x}^{2}$, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that 
${x}^{2}=u-1.$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{5}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{4}\cdot \sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & =\int (u-1)^{2}\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (u-1)^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

q-113752.worked_solution:
Let $u=2x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{u+1}{2}.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{u+1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{u\sqrt{u}+\sqrt{u}}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int ({u}^{3/2}+{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}+\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(2x-1)^{5/2}+\frac{1}{6}(2x-1)^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\sqrt{(2x-1)^{5}}+\frac{1}{6}\sqrt{(2x-1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{1}{2}(u-1).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1/2$ | $3/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $4$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/2}^{3/2}4x\sqrt{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(u-1)\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={(\frac{1}{(5/2)}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{1}{(3/2)}{u}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & ={(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {4}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {4}^{3/2})-(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {0}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {0}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{112}{15}\end{aligned}
$$
